title: IB Maths AI Past Papers: A Final-Weeks Plan
summary: IB Maths AI past papers become useful when you time attempts, self-mark honestly, log errors, repair weak topics, and retest them calmly before exam day.
body_markdown:
The final weeks before an IB Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation exam are the time to turn what you know into marks. Use older exam papers as a feedback system: attempt, mark, diagnose, repair and retest. Completing more questions helps only when the next session addresses what the previous one revealed.


A useful revision loop is simple:


- Complete a timed paper or selected section.
- Self-mark against the relevant IB Maths AI markscheme.
- Record the cause of each lost mark.
- Repair the weakness through focused practice.
- Reattempt missed questions independently.
- Test the improvement under timed conditions.


### Begin with a timed diagnostic


Your first attempt provides evidence about your current performance. Clear your desk, silence your phone and use the calculator and formula booklet permitted for your course. Work without notes. RevisionDojo's guide to[time management in IB Math exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-master-time-management-in-ib-math-exams) can help you establish checkpoints.


When time finishes, stop and mark unfinished parts. The difference between what you can solve eventually and what you can complete within the limit matters.


Record your raw mark, unattempted marks, method marks lost and avoidable errors. These measures separate pacing problems from mathematical weaknesses. Avoid treating one score as a predicted grade: difficulty and grade boundaries vary. Look instead for recurring causes you can address.


Choose material that matches your level and current course. If an older question uses unfamiliar content or instructions, check its relevance with your teacher before treating it as a weakness. A diagnostic helps most when it measures skills you are actually expected to demonstrate.


### Make the markscheme part of revision


A markscheme shows which mathematical evidence earns credit. Applications and Interpretation markschemes use annotations including M, A and R, broadly associated with method, accuracy and reasoning. Follow the requirements of the individual question when awarding marks.


Mark in another colour and compare your written solution with each credited step. Write the missing requirement beside each error. A correct calculator result does not automatically demonstrate every required equation, explanation or contextual conclusion.


Be strict about what appears on the page. Reasoning you intended to write cannot help an examiner assess your response. If an alternative method seems valid but you cannot judge its treatment confidently, ask your teacher.


RevisionDojo's guide to[analysing IB Math AA and AI markschemes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-analyze-markschemes-for-ib-math-aa-and-ai) explains how marking can inform clearer solutions.


A student asks a calculator for an answer while another student points out that the examiner wants to see the working.


### Turn errors into decisions


“Statistics mistake” does not tell you what to practise tomorrow. An effective error log identifies the precise obstacle and gives it a repair action.


Error type Practical repair


Knowledge gap Review the concept and answer focused questions


Method gap Study a solution, then reproduce the approach independently


Calculator gap Repeat the exact calculator workflow


Interpretation gap Practise conclusions with units and contextual language


Accuracy error Retain calculator precision and check copied values


Timing error Practise moving on and returning later


For each entry, record the topic, question reference, marks lost, cause, repair date and retest date. Keep descriptions specific: “selected the wrong regression model” is more useful than “calculator problem.”


Review the log before choosing your next session. Several lost marks may share one cause, such as premature rounding. Fixing that habit can improve performance across otherwise unrelated topics.


Prioritise errors that recur, affect several questions or block an otherwise familiar method. For example, repeated trouble entering data deserves attention before an isolated arithmetic slip. Choose one or two priorities per session so that reviewing the log leads directly to work you can finish.


### Repair weak topics between attempts


Another complete paper is useful once you have acted on the previous attempt. Between timed sessions, concentrate on the topics and habits your error log identifies.


The[RevisionDojo Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/questionbank) supports focused practice, while the guide to[targeted IB Math revision](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-use-the-questionbank-for-targeted-math-revision) helps turn broad weaknesses into manageable question sets.


Try this repair block:


- Review relevant Study Notes for 15-20 minutes.
- Answer three accessible questions to rebuild the method.
- Complete three exam-style questions without notes.
- Mark your work and update the log.
- Return to the original missed question later.


Use Flashcards for definitions and conditions. Ask AI Chat why a method applies, then complete the work yourself. Grading tools can help you examine missing reasoning; Tutors can help resolve persistent misconceptions. Keep the Coursework Library for separate coursework needs so examination revision stays focused.


For SL students, these[IB Math AI self-study resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-math-ai-sl-resources-self-study) offer further guidance on balancing topic learning and assessment practice.


### Retest without support


A solution can look obvious immediately after you read it. Test your understanding after at least one intervening study session, starting from a blank page.


If you remember the answer, choose a parallel question. The task is to retrieve and select the method independently. Classify the result as secure, developing or unresolved. Secure means accurate work with clear reasoning; developing means you still needed a prompt; unresolved means further repair is necessary.


Return unresolved questions to focused practice. Check secure skills again within mixed sets, where the topic is not announced. This tests method selection alongside execution.


### Return to complete timed practice


As the examination approaches, include complete timed attempts to practise concentration, pacing and recovery after difficult questions. Use Mock Exams or Predicted Papers as practice material, without assuming they forecast examination content. The guide to[combining exam practice with AI tools](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/optimizing-ib-exam-preparation-official-papers-ai-tools) provides a framework for connecting attempts with feedback.


Before starting, decide how you will respond when progress stalls. Mark the question, leave readable working and move to another part when appropriate. During review, check whether this decision protected time for accessible marks or whether you abandoned a question you could have completed.


HL students should include extended problem solving appropriate to Paper 3. Define variables, organise information and carry valid results forward. For further reflection on precision and interpretation, read about[improving performance in IB Math AI](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/difference-between-6-and-7-ib-math-ai) .


### Keep the final days manageable


Alternate performance and repair, then reduce volume in the final days. Review recurring errors, rehearse essential calculator workflows, organise permitted equipment and protect sleep.


RevisionDojo brings the cycle together through Questionbank practice, Study Notes, Flashcards and feedback. Choose each resource because it addresses a specific need. A completed paper becomes valuable when its evidence changes what you do next.
